_source.Proposal Title: Comparison of Structure and Segregation in Alloys Directionally Solidified in Terrestrial and Microgravity Environments
_source.Objectives: The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand how the intensity of convection and the direction of the flow influences the evolution of the mushy zone, macro- and micro-segregation, morphology of dendrites, the growth mode and spatial arrangement of intermetallic precipitates.
_source.Approach: 3 different Al-Si alloys were directionally solidified under different thermal gradient and furnace translation velocities. Along with micro and macro-segregation, dendritic characteristics including primary arm spacing and trunk diameters were quantified. Microgravity results were compared to those obtained under terrestrial conditions. A finite volume modeling approach was undertaken in the absence of convection and predictions were compared to data obtained from microgravity and terrestrial samples.
_source.Hypothesis: Dendritic metrics of the directionally solidified (DS) samples are expected to have dendritic characteristics that compare very well to model predictions for growth in the absence of convection. Earth-grown samples are not anticipated to compare well, indicating that the convection in Earth grown alloys does indeed play a role in microstructural development during the solidification process. Further, Earth-grown samples exhibit a type of macrosegregation called ''steepling” in which the periphery of a DS-ed sample is of eutectic composition and is seen in alloys with solutes that increase the density of the liquid during solidification. Samples grown aboard the ISS are not expected to have steepling.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The research is relevant to a process known as directional solidification, which is used for producing critical castings that are used in gas turbine engines. Gas turbine engines power aircraft (i.e., often called ''jet engines'') and are also used to generate electric power. These castings are made of vacuum melted alloys that are capable of withstanding the demanding conditions at high temperatures and consequently the metallurgical structure of the alloys must be of the highest quality. The research is leading to an improved understanding of how microstructures and segregation form in directionally solidified castings; hence the science of producing such castings will be enhanced as a result of the research. In addition, the research findings relate to many other types of castings, including billets and ingots, of alloys (i.e., steel, aluminum alloys, etc.) that are critical for metal fabrication. In addition, the benchmark microgravity data allows validation of models predicting dendritic metrics such as primary and secondary arm spacing and trunk diameter. Such validated simulation models can enable optimization of casting parameters.

_source.Title: SUBSA Brazing of Aluminum Alloys IN Space
_source.Keywords: Brazing     Microgravity     Buoyancy     Aluminum     Capillary Flow     Wetting
_source.Objectives: The primary scientific goal of the proposed  terrestrial and planned microgravity molten metal  capillary flow experiments is to better understand the physics of the flow of molten metals over the topographically modified surfaces (e.g., filling in the holes, flow over sharp edges and/or flow over surfaces having variable curvatures). By performing capillary flow tests both on Earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of microgravity on the kinetics of the larger masses of melt flow, and ultimate equilibrium shape of the meniscus will be closely examined. The objective of the microgravity experiments is to provide benchmark data against which theoretical models and computer simulations can be tested. The BRAINS project’s primary pragmatic/engineering obective is that a capillary flow of braze under microgravity conditions would enable a repair or bonding of larger and/or more irregular mating surfaces defects, compared to the terrestrial conditions. This would be important for future development of advanced brazing techniques with applications to both damage repair and construction in space.
_source.Approach: Before being assembled into the ampoule, the samples were always ultrasonically cleaned in the sequence of (i) soapy water, (ii) water, (iii) 190 proof ethanol, and then dried in air or a compressed air. A double nitrogen purge was done before sealing the ampoule. Three configurations of the Al alloy filler and corresponding substrates were considered as relevant for the intended study: (i) HOLE, (ii) PIN and (iii) Hollow Pin. Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules” (SUBSA) furnace, which was designed for operation in the ISS’s Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) was used for this investigation. All samples were placed in the isothermal region of the furnace instrumented with thermocouples. The furnace was heated to the dwell temperature (600 - 605 °C ± 2K) at a rate of 5 K/minute (optimal 10K/minute). A dwell time was maintained for completion of capillary flow and establishing of the equilibrium meniscus shape. Subsequent cooling of the samples was performed at the maximum cooling rate allowed by the facility. Capillary topography identification and microstructure evaluation was performed on all samples.
_source.Hypothesis: A series of space (ISS) and terrestrial experiments, integrated with modeling and analysis are expected to answer the following practical and fundamental questions: (1) How can the absence of gravity and dominance of capillary forces be take advantage of in transporting the molten braze? (2) Which brazing alloy and the brazing technique will enable strong and efficient bonding of selected proxies of structural elements and facilitate a repair. That is, can brazing be done in space and/or on board of space vehicles by using flux-less braze? Specifically: A comparison between flux and flux-less brazing under space and terrestrial conditions can answer underlying scientific questions related to molten metal flow kinetics, specifically wetting and spreading of liquid clad/filler over topographically modified surfaces.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: A brazing process may be used to mitigate the consequences of high velocity micro meteoroids’ and/or space debris’ impacts, and possible catastrophic penetration of aluminum man-made objects in space. Second, construction in space would necessitate joining complex assemblies, e.g., habitat systems, with brazing being one meaningful manufacturing option of permanent bonding. Validation fundamental models including phase field models will allow prediction of terrestrial brazing quality.

_source.Proposal Title: Plasma crystal research on the ISS
_source.Objectives:
Plasma crystals are a new kind of matter, rediscovered in 1994. They form under certain conditions in a complex (dusty) plasma. There, the electrically charged dust particles arrange in a regular macroscopic crystal lattice. This structure allows for an investigation of the properties of condensed matter on the kinetic level. This means that basic processes, such as melting, can be followed by observing the motion of individual particles. PK-3 will give investigators a better understanding of plasma in space and will determine the critical points for the plasma.

Gravity plays an important role for the structure of plasma crystals. In microgravity large 3-dimensional plasma crystals can be grown and studied in detail on the most fundamental, the kinetic level. Complex plasmas can be seen as model systems for the investigation of fundamental phenomena in liquids and crystals and provide information on the motion of single particles (“atoms”). This provides new insights into the field of condensed matter.
_source.Approach:
PK-3 Plus is a symmetrical driven radio-frequency plasma discharge with special features for the investigation of complex plasmas under microgravity conditions. As a second generation laboratory, PK-3 Plus provides major new possibilities for these investigations due to its design improvements relative to the first long-term experiment PKE-Nefedov. The PK-3 Plus apparatus allows investigations at neutral gas pressures between 0.05 - 2.5 millibar and radio frequency (rf) power of 0.01 - 1 W. The complex plasma can consist of monodisperse particles in a size range from 1 - 20 micrometers. Up to six particle sizes can be added to the experimental volume. It is possible to change the number of particles, the composition of particles, the plasma conditions and the neutral gas pressure during one experiment. The particle cloud can be excited by an electrical low frequency signal on the electrodes (0.1 - 100 Hz at a maximum amplitude of 50 V) or by a low frequency modulation of the rf-amplitude in different wave forms (sinusoidal, square, pulse, etc.).

The PK-3 Plus investigation has two major pieces of equipment: the experimental block, and the telescience system (TS). The research will be performed on the ISS inside the plasma chamber situated inside of the experimental block. The experimental block is attached via a tube to the space environment to produce the prevacuum for turbomolecular pump, which can produce pressure in the plasma chamber less than 10-5 millibar.

The TS is the computer in which the chamber conditions can be altered via actuators in the experimental block and the storage unit for the data collected. This PK3 Plus laboratory has state of the art hardware and software, and provides better diagnostics than previous hardware. The PK-3 Plus laboratory was operated on the Russian segment of ISS by Russian cosmonauts mostly.

Typical experimental campaigns have 3 or 4 runs to meet the requirements of the investigator. There are two modes, automatic and manual, for this investigation. During the manual mode, crew time will be required to complete the investigation. Experimenters are following live video transmission from the experimental block in the control center in Korolev guiding the cosmonaut via audio contact for experiment parameters optimization. Full set Recorded videos and housekeeping data are to be returned on hard drives via Soyuz capsule.

The experiments run on three or four consecutive days during single experimental campaign. Some days areon automatic, as mentioned above, and some days are manual operations, depending on the cosmonaut availability and investigators plans. On automatic days, the machine can be left alone to run, passively taking measurements of the complex plasma behaviors under microgravity. On the manual day, there will be a cosmonaut present, adjusting settings to achieve the required states of the plasma. The experiment is expected to take approximately 90 minutes each day.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: 99% of the visible matter in the universe is in the plasma state and dust is ubiquitous, too. Thus so called dusty plasmas can be found in interstellar media, in planetary forming discs, in cometary atmospheres, in Saturn rings, etc. The results from the PK-3 Plus laboratory on the ISS on the charging of the microparticles/dust and their interaction with each other and the surrounding plasma, the so-called basic fundamental questions, are very helpful in the understanding of dusty plasmas in space. Additionally, complex plasmas are models for liquid and crystalline systems providing new insights into the formation and behavior of condensed matter.

_source.Proposal Title: Growth Rate Dispersion as a Predictive Indicator for Biological Crystal Samples Where Quality Can be Improved with Microgravity Growth
_source.Objectives:
The primary objectives of this investigation are:
1. Use molecular biology to produce closely related protein constructs that display differences in growth rate dispersion during crystallization. Measure the intermolecular ‘attractiveness’ of each construct, then model the inter-particle forces, diffusion and convection.
2. Measure and compare the growth rate dispersion of ground and microgravity grown crystals. Growth rate dispersion will be measured for ground control crystals using routine crystallization apparatus. In addition, growth rate dispersion will be measure for ground and
microgravity grown crystals using the flight apparatus.
3. Characterize the quality of both ground and microgravity grown crystals. Sophisticated X-ray analysis along with X-ray structural data collection will be used to quantify and characterize crystal quality.
 4. Link the knowledge about inter-particle forces, measured acceleration levels, calculated flow rates and the resultant X-ray analysis to develop a model and predictive ground-based tests to identify those samples producing crystals on the ground that would be improved in microgravity.
_source.Approach:
Approach: Several cassettes were configured with cassettes identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18. Six constructs and the T4 wild type (WT) were loaded into the capillaries at various concentrations and frozen to -80C. The samples were thawed and observed in the LMM facility on board the ISS.

Several cassettes were identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18. The capillaries were loaded so that capillaries 1-6 contained theWT* construct, capillaries 7-12 the S44E WT* construct and finally, capillaries 13-18 the S44F WT* construct. The cassettes were kept at -80°C until moving to the space station microscope facility. The capillaries were filled as follows:
• Capillaries 1-6 with 50 mg/ml WT* in 0.1 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M Tris, pH 8, 35% PEG 8K, and 0.1 M NaCl
• Capillaries 7-12 with 64 mg/ml S44E WT* in 0.05 M NaC 2 H3 O2 0.1 M Tris, pH 8 30% PEG 8K and 15% glycerol
• Capillaries 13-18 with 53 mg/ml S44F WT* in 0.2 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M NaC2H3O2, pH 5 and 20% PEG 20K.
On return to earth X-ray analysis of samples took place using the IMCA (Industrial Macromolecular Crystallography Association) beamline of the Advanced Photon Source.
_source.Hypothesis:
Removing or greatly reducing the effects of buoyancy-driven convection and sedimentation in microgravity will result in slower, diffusion-controlled molecular transport that can yield larger crystals with fewer defects.
It is postulated that growth rate dispersion is reduced in microgravity due to the diffusive rather than convective flow regime that delivers macromolecules to the crystal. Based on previous experimental observations it is hypothesized that the presence of growth rate dispersion in macromolecular crystals grown on the ground is an indicator of crystals that can be improved when grown in microgravity.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: X-ray crystallography is the main method scientists use to study the molecular structures of biology, but it is difficult to crystallize proteins, with only a poor success rate even in the best laboratories. This investigation uses ground and microgravity-based observations to predict which proteins would benefit from crystallization in microgravity, improving the information that may be obtained from them.

Long-duration protein crystal growth experiments on the ISS with photo documentation, and subsequent analysis of the comparisons between 1g and μg crystals, will enable a more complete understanding of why proteins and other macromolecules often form more perfect crystals in microgravity than they do on earth. If it could be predicted which macromolecular samples could be improved by crystal growth in microgravity, then the true potential of this medium could be exploited in an efficient manner. Structural biology of protein-protein complexes and integral membrane proteins are currently a high NIH priority due to their importance for systems biology, disease mechanisms and structure-guided drug development. Hauptman Woodward Medical Research Institute has a data archive of millions of time-resolved crystallization images (from over 14,000 different biological macromolecules) that could be used to identify candidates likely to benefit from crystallization in microgravity.

_source.Title: DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization - Alice Like Insert
_source.Keywords: Crystals     gas-liquid transformation     Crystallization     French Space Agency
_source.Objectives:
Identify and clarify the different growth mechanisms in fluid systems where hydrodynamics is relevant, particularly during phase separation near the critical point.

To investigate the role of fluctuating hydrodynamics (Brownian motion and local hydrodynamic interactions) in the coarsening of domains, especially when the equilibrium volume fraction of the new phase is minimal.

To analyze the growth kinetics of new experiments performed at very low volume fractions, taking into account fluctuation relaxation effects and Brownian motion within a hydrodynamic framework.

To investigate phase transitions induced by mechanical quenches (density variations using a piston), a novel approach contrasting with traditional temperature quenches.

To study the phase transition kinetics when the fluid is submitted to external vibration in low-g.
_source.Approach: The investigation approach for DECLIC-ALI centers on conducting experiments within the microgravity environment of the ISS, utilizing the DECLIC facility and its specialized Alice-Like Insert (ALI, ALI-R, and ALI-2). The approach involves precise control of the temperature and density of the SF6 sample, including temperature and mechanical quenches, as well as heat pulse techniques. A suite of optical diagnostics (Interferometry, shadowgraphy, light scattering, and direct observation) is used to visualize and quantify the SF6 fluid behavior. Different sample cell configurations, including fixed and variable volume cells, are employed within the ALI insert. Data acquisition is performed at high frequencies, and the data are analyzed quantitatively, with a strong emphasis on comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions. The overall approach is iterative, building upon previous space-based experiments and refining both experimental techniques and theoretical models, all focused on understanding the critical phenomena of SF6.
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that fluctuating hydrodynamics will dominate domain growth at low volume fractions, challenging classical theories. A sharp transition between growth regimes is expected. Mechanical quenches are hypothesized to be a viable method for inducing phase ordering. The vapor recoil force is believed to significantly influence bubble dynamics and wetting near the critical point. Adiabatic volume changes are expected to reveal the dynamics of the Piston Effect. Critical water is hypothesized to follow the same universality class, and external vibration will affect the dynamics.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The DECLIC facility provides power, communications, command, control, data storage, and multiple, flexible optical capabilities in support of each experiment. The knowledge gained will assist in the understanding of the behavior of cryogenic (of or relating to very low temperatures) rocket propellants for the study of dynamics regarding near-ambient temperature critical fluids. DECLIC is designed for telescience from the ground and will offer scientists the capability to remotely control experiment conditions onboard the ISS provided by DECLIC lockers. The use of near-critical fluids allows important parameters (e.g., compressibility of supercritical fluids, density of gas and liquid phases, surface tension) to be easily varied in a scaled way by using small changes in temperature. The readily variable properties of near-critical fluids makes them appealing candidates for studying numerous interesting phenomena valid for all fluids, which will ultimately leads to the development of improved solvents for chemistry and the environment.

_source.Title: Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 1
_source.Keywords: Capillary Channel Flow     CCF     Capillary Flow
_source.Objectives: The investigation aims to characterize and quantify critical flow dynamics in open capillary channels of parallel plate and groove geometries. A primary objective is determining the critical flow rates at which free surface destabilization (''choking'') and gas ingestion occur, emphasizing the capillary-inertial regime. The investigation will examine the relationship between critical flow rate and channel length for complete and half-channel configurations. Controlled, low-frequency flow oscillations will be introduced to probe instability onset sensitivity across geometries and lengths. High-fidelity data on free surface shapes and critical velocities will be acquired to validate theoretical models and assess underlying assumptions, refining predictive capabilities for capillary flows relevant to spacecraft fluid management.
_source.Approach: The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initally, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology builtinto the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs.
_source.Hypothesis: The primary hypothesis guiding CCF-CV EU1 is that a limiting flow rate, or 'choking' phenomenon, exists in open capillary channels with parallel plate and groove geometries. A relationship between the fluid velocity, the channel geometry, and the fluid properties governs this limit. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the introduction of wave oscillations within the flow will impact the critical flow rate, with the amplitude and frequency of these oscillations playing a significant role in the flow behavior and the onset of choking.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
The knowledge of liquid management in space is important for any device which contain liquid and gas, and have one or many free liquid surfaces. The requirements for the device which experiences different acceleration levels down to fully compensated gravity conditions (weightlessness) during its operation may include the phase separation of liquid from gas, gas from liquid, and the transport of liquid through liquid acquisition devices. The results from the CCF experiments may help to design subsystems of future spacecrafts, such as the propulsion subsystem, the thermal control subsystem and the life support subsystem for crewed exploration. The data can be used to build mathematical models which can be applied to real fluids and real dimensions. The data can be used as well to validate computational fluid dynamics software packages which are state-of-the-art tools the design of spacecrafts.
Capillary forces on Earth are masked by gravity, but may become dominant in small scales. This can be encountered when a wetting liquid wicks into a porous structure. It may be a wanted - as in the case of cleaning - or an unwanted - as in buildings - effect. In a wider sense the CCF experiments contribute to this topic. The main difference is that the flow was not driven by the capillary forces. Instead, the capillary forces were used to stabilize the flow path. A variety of applications on Earth may have this requirement as well.

_source.Title: Pool Boiling Experiment
_source.Keywords: Pool Boiling Experiment     Heat Flux     Bubble Growth     PBE     Nucleate Pool Boiling
_source.Objectives:
The program described here seeks to improve the understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that constitute nucleate pool boiling. The vehicle for accomplishing this is an investigation, including experiments to be conducted in microgravity and coupled with appropriate analyses, of the heat transfer and vapor bubble dynamics associated with nucleation, bubble growth or collapse, and subsequent motion. Certain effects that can be neglected at normal Earth gravity, such as surface tension and vapor momentum, can become quite significant in microgravity. Momentum imparted to the liquid by the vapor bubble during growth tends to draw the vapor bubble away from the surface, depending on the rate of growth, which in turn is governed by the temperature distribution in the liquid. Thermophoretic forces, arising from the variation of the liquid-vapor surface tension with temperature, on the other hand, tend to move the vapor bubble toward the region of higher temperature. The bubble motion will be governed by which of these two effects prevail.

The elements of nucleate boiling, for which research conducted under microgravity would advance the basic understanding, are:
   1. Nucleation or onset of boiling. Indications are that both heater surface temperature and temperature distribution in the liquid are necessary to describe nucleation.
   2. The dynamic growth of a vapor bubble in the vicinity of the heater surface. This includes the shape as well as motion of the liquid-vapor interface as growth is taking place. These are influenced by the liquid
   temperature distribution at the initiation of growth.
   3. The subsequent behavior of the vapor bubble. This includes the motion, whether departure takes place or not, and the associated heat transfer.
_source.Approach:
The approach encompasses a comprehensive experimental methodology designed to dissect the nuances of the boiling process in an environment where gravity's influence is minimal. This approach aims to isolate and analyze the core mechanisms that drive nucleate pool boiling, offering insights that are obscured under normal Earth gravity conditions.

Here is an outline of the investigation's methodological approach:
1. Experimental Setup in Microgravity:
   a. The investigation utilizes a specially designed experimental apparatus capable of accurately controlling and measuring heat flux, liquid subcooling levels, and temperature distribution within the liquid and at
   the heater surface. This apparatus is deployed in a microgravity environment provided by space-based platforms to ensure the minimization of gravity's influence on the boiling process.

2. Controlled Heat Flux Application:
   a. A key component of the approach involves applying a controlled heat flux to a pool of liquid, initiating the boiling process. The heat flux is carefully modulated to explore a range of boiling conditions, from
   gentle nucleation to vigorous boiling, under varying levels of liquid subcooling.

3. High-Resolution Data Acquisition:
   a. To capture the dynamics of bubble formation, growth, and departure, the investigation employs high-resolution, high-speed imaging techniques, along with precise temperature and heat flux measurement
   tools. This data acquisition setup allows for the detailed observation and analysis of bubble behavior and heat transfer phenomena during the boiling process.

4. Parameter Variation:
   a. The investigation systematically varies key parameters, including the heat flux magnitude, the degree of liquid subcooling, and the pressure within the system, to study their effects on the nucleation process,
   bubble dynamics, and heat transfer rates. This parameter variation helps in identifying the critical factors that influence nucleate pool boiling under microgravity.

5. Data Analysis and Model Development:
   a. The collected data undergoes rigorous analysis to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms of nucleate pool boiling, focusing on nucleation criteria, bubble growth rates, and heat transfer characteristics.
   Insights gained from the analysis are used to develop and refine predictive models that can accurately describe boiling behavior under a variety of conditions.

6. Cross-Comparison with Earth Gravity Data:
   a. Findings from the microgravity experiments are compared with data obtained from similar experiments conducted under Earth gravity conditions. This cross-comparison aids in isolating the effects of gravity
   on the boiling process and contributes to the development of generalized models that can predict boiling behavior across different gravitational environments.

_source.Objectives:
Specific objectives of this investigation were as follows:
   • Plan and develop experiment parameter sets to investigate anomalous nucleation events in zirconium samples during ISS-EML experiments
   • Analyze cavitation-induced nucleation experiments on zirconium and zirconium-nickel alloys
   • Analyze fluid flow during ISS-EML experiments to support collaborators investigations
   • Continue flight preparations and development of experimental parameter sets for upcoming experiments in Batch 3
   • Provide magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modeling support of macroconvection in various materials for three ESA sponsored projects: PARSEC, THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL.
_source.Approach:
• The anomalous nucleation events of interest are hypothesized to be caused by cavitation in the melt. Experiments replicated the conditions in which the nucleation events were previously observed and explored similar experimental conditions.
• Magnetohydrodynamic modeling of fluid flow is to be used to determine the flow conditions during ISS-EML experiments. Relevant parameters include fluid velocity, shear rates, turbulence intensity, and their distribution. Such data is critical for control of experiments and input to other theoretical and modeling efforts.
_source.Hypothesis:
• Dynamic nucleation is an effect of the fluid flow and not reliant on classical nucleation theory.
• Thermophysical property measurements may require appropriate flow conditions, which should be quantified
• Flow conditions may affect solidification and nucleation behavior
• Oxygen may influence surface tension measurements in metallic melts
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Containerless processing provides access to the deeply undercooled region of metallic melts. Using this unique processing environement we are able to investigate fundamental solidification behaivor and meausure thermophysical properties of metallic melts including density, surface tension, viscosity, thermal expansion, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and electrical conductivity. More specifically, impacts and benefits are broken out by the 3 associated flight experiments.

In PARSEC,  the effect of fluid flow on the solidification path of certain alloys is investigated. Control of the solidification path would enable tailoring of the microstructure and properties of metal parts for specific applications.

In ThermoLAB, the thermophysical properties of high-temperature materials is investigated. Many of these materials are used commercially. A better understanding of the physical properties will allow more efficient and more reliable production of metallic parts using these alloys. Other alloys are chosen because of scientific interest in their properties, which may illuminate fundamental physics related to the formation of bulk metallic glasses and quasicrystals.

The nucleation and growth of quasicrystals, and the effect of atomic-scale order on the macroscopic properties of these alloys is investigated in ICOPROSOL. This fundamental investigation may improve our ability to tailor the microstructure of metals for commercial applications.

_source.Title: Nucleate Pool Boiling eXperiment
_source.Keywords: Bubble Dynamics     Boiling
_source.Objectives:
The primary objective of the proposed study is to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate boiling under microgravity conditions. Specific objectives included:
- Single bubble dynamics (nucleation, growth, and departure) under microgravity conditions under constant wall temperature.
- Effect of liquid subcooling, wall superheat, and system pressure on single bubble dynamics.
- Heat flux variation on the heated surface during single bubble evolution.
- Lateral merger of bubbles formed at neighboring sites and mechanism of vapor removal from the surface.
_source.Approach:
The research utilized a systematic and comprehensive approach to understand the complexities of nucleate pool boiling in a microgravity environment. The approach was characterized by a strategic ''building block'' strategy, progressing from simpler to more complex scenarios, enabling a gradual and insightful understanding of the underlying physics.

Here's a detailed breakdown of the investigation approach:

1. Single Bubble Dynamics:

The research commenced by focusing on the behavior of a single bubble nucleating from a pre-fabricated cavity on the aluminum wafer. This fundamental building block allowed for a detailed examination of bubble growth, departure (if any), and the associated heat transfer processes in microgravity conditions.

2. Multiple Bubble Mergers:

Building upon the knowledge gained from single bubble studies, the investigation then explored the interactions of multiple bubbles. Experiments were conducted to study the merger of bubbles nucleating from different cavities. This stage investigated how bubbles merge in the lateral direction, the mechanisms of vapor removal from the heated surface after merger, and the impact of these interactions on the overall heat transfer rates.

3. Integral Nucleate Boiling:

The investigation then broadened its scope by conducting experiments with boiling occurring over the entire heater surface. This aimed to obtain the boiling curve, which depicts the relationship between heat flux and wall superheat, under microgravity conditions. This provided a macroscopic view of nucleate pool boiling, considering the collective behavior of numerous bubbles.

4. Numerical Simulations:

The experimental work was tightly coupled with complete numerical simulations of the boiling process. These simulations employed advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques to capture the intricate details of bubble dynamics and heat transfer. The simulations accounted for a range of factors including time-varying system pressure and temperatures, the presence of dissolved gas in the liquid, surface tension effects, and the influence of microlayer evaporation. The numerical model was rigorously validated against the experimental data obtained in the NPBX experiments.

5. Model Development:

The ultimate goal of the research was to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate pool boiling heat transfer under microgravity conditions. This model, based on the physical understanding derived from experimental observations and validated numerical simulations, aimed to provide a reliable tool for predicting boiling behavior across a wide range of parameters and conditions relevant to space applications.
_source.Hypothesis: In microgravity conditions, where buoyancy forces become negligible, it is expected that forces arising from the inertia of the liquid, evaporation, and condensation at the vapor-liquid interface, disjoining pressure, capillary pressure gradient, and the resulting flow field will become more dominant. The study aimed to understand and quantify the effect of these forces and identify the conditions under which quasi-static or steady-state boiling is possible under prolonged microgravity duration.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
While the primary motivation for this investigation was to advance our understanding of boiling heat transfer in the context of space applications, the knowledge gained has significant implications for Earth-based technologies and scientific understanding as well.

Here are some key potential impacts and benefits:

1. Improved Understanding of Boiling at Earth Gravity:

By studying boiling in a microgravity environment where buoyancy forces are negligible, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the interplay of other forces and phenomena that influence boiling behavior. This knowledge can, in turn, enhance our comprehension of boiling processes under Earth's gravity, where buoyancy often masks the effects of these more subtle factors.

2. Development of More Efficient Heat Transfer Systems:

The insights gained from this research can contribute to the development of more efficient boiling heat transfer systems for a wide range of applications on Earth. Enhanced efficiency translates to reduced energy consumption, lower operational costs, and a reduced environmental footprint.

3. Advancements in Miniaturization of Electronics:

As electronic devices continue to shrink in size, effective thermal management becomes increasingly critical. Understanding boiling in microgravity is crucial for developing innovative cooling solutions for miniaturized electronics, as these devices often operate at high heat fluxes and face challenges in dissipating heat effectively.

4. New Insights into Fluid Physics:

This research offers valuable insights into fundamental fluid physics phenomena, including the behavior of bubbles, interfacial phenomena, and the dynamics of multiphase flows. This knowledge can lead to advancements in diverse fields, such as materials science, biomedical engineering, and environmental science.

_source.Title: Round Robin - Thermophysical Property Measurement
_source.Keywords: Electrostatic levitation     Super Alloys     Thermophysical Properties     Round Robin     pure metals     Uncertainty Analysis     ELF     A-Plus
_source.Proposal Title: Round Robin: Thermophysical Property Measurement, Augmented-Program for Levitation Utilization in Space (A-PLUS)
_source.Objectives:
The key scientific objectives are:
   (a) Conducting baseline space ESL containerless property measurement experiments for two paired classes of levitation-based thermophysical properties:Density/Thermal Expansion, Viscosity/Surface Tension.
   (b) Selecting materials compatible with both electrostatic levitation (ESL) and electromagnetic levitation (EML) to allow comparison between space facilities.
   (c) Using modeling to evaluate theories used to predict the influence of gravity on propertymeasurement experiments.
   (d) Actively encouraging collaboration with existing science teams using other facilities through organizing a Round Robin test consortium
_source.Approach:
The experimental approach involved inserting a sample carousel of 20 individual samples into the JAXA ISS-ELF facility, conditioning the test atmosphere, and conducting individual melt cycles on each sample. The heating lasers were used to precondition the sample when the sample is heated to a desired pre-bake temperature. Following the preconditioning period, the sample was charged by the electrodes and released to achieve stable positioning. The lasers were then used to thermally cycle the sample. The cycle starts by application of the highest laser heating power (activated by a control current setting in the ELF software measured in amps) until the sample is fully molten and achieved the maximum liquid superheat temperature. The heater power was then turned down to maintain the desired isothermal hold. Surface excitation was conducted using varying volage from the electrodes at this temperature. Surface tension and viscosity was measured using the droplet oscillation behavior. The laser power was then turned off to allow the molten sample to cool down. Density and cp/ε evaluations are conducted during the free cooling without any influence from the laser. Once recalescence occurred, the sample was then allowed to become fully solid at room temperature which marks the completion of a thermal cycle. Overall, processing a single melt cycle can take up to 10 - 15 minutes excluding the pre-bake. Following the cycle completion, the sample is retrieved back into the cartridge to end the test on this sample.

Using the described experimental approach several thermophysical properties were measured on a variety of metallic melts as described below:
1.	 Density –One high-speed video camera was used to monitor the sample size as a function of time during the free cooling phase. Sample edge was detected using a custom algorithm for the density measurement. The volume of the sample was calculated using a known calibration of pixels/mm3, which was subsequently correlated with temperature allowing calculation of density and thermal expansion coefficient (from the slope of the density curve). Tracking of sample mass loss was accomplished post-mission using Langmuir’s equation of evaporation.
2.	 Surface tension – After melting, the heating laser is set to a reduced value such that the sample is held at constant temperature. A sinusoidal modulation of the positioning voltage was applied to both electrodes to excite surface oscillations without changing sample position. The resulting sample deformation was measured by the high-speed linear array. A frequeny sweep was conducted to identify natural frequency. Two method was applied to identify the natural frequency from the sweep: (1) Maximum amplitude method where maximum deformation is observed at the natural frequency and (2) Excitation crossover method where the natural frequency was observed at the linear intersections  of the damped and free oscillations.  Natural frequencies identified using both methods were used to evaluate the surface tension.
3.	Viscosity – In conjunction to surface tension, viscosity was measured from the damped oscillations at the identified natural frequency. The characteristic exponential time decay from a sinusoidal fit was used to evaluate the viscosity.
4.	Specific heat capacity and emissivity – The ratio of these two quantities was evaluated from the cooling curve as monitored by the IR pyrometer after correction for conductive mass losses to the gas environment.
5.	Evaporation – Integration of the time-temperature profile allows calculation of evaporation assuming a known relationship using Langmuir’s equation for loss as a function of temperature. Pre- and post- measurement of sample mass anchors these predictions. Dynamic mass is crucial for tracking for density, surface tension and viscosity measurement.
_source.Hypothesis: The experimental hypothesis was that in microgravity environment in the absence of stirring, high quality thermophysical property would be measured compared to the ground-based levitation facility. This was successfully observed for gold samples.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This research aids in dissemination of an baseline archived dataset allowing researchers to validate models accounting for gravity-induced systematic error in property measurement used for industrial welding, casting  and additive manufacturing operations . Industry will be better able to correlate ground and space results to expand the quantity and quality of available information without the requirement for access to space. Advance the understanding of how to best allocate the scant resources available for space-based materials property measurement using levitation.  In the future this could lead to development of a model where fidelity and cost can be readily calculated for a given material classification and serve as the basis for prioritization of specific ground and space thermophysical property investigations.

_source.Proposal Title: Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
_source.Objectives:
A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence):
    Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios   (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.
    Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
    Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.
_source.Approach:
A series of experiments is proposed in which mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will be issued into an oxidizing environment through a spherical porous burner and ignited to obtain, nominally, a spherical, one-dimensional stabilized flame. Synchronized measurements are to be made including spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux measurements, and system operating conditions (including reactant flow rates, ambient temperatures, pressures and acceleration levels, etc.). These data are to be used for comparisons of flame behavior and structure with detailed numerical simulations of the flames.
Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an important intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons. Diluents mixed with fuel are to include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities, and carbon dioxide to influence flame radiation characteristics.
_source.Hypothesis:
The transient numerical simulation of spherical flames developed as part of this program includes detailed chemistry and transport models, especially radiation mechanisms. Each description of the flames obtained from the experiment, including measurements of aspects of the flame structure, growth or flame front velocities, and the specific test conditions where steady state flames, flame extinctions, flame front instabilities, soot suppression limits, etc., comprise a rigorous test of the detailed model. Together they provide a measure of the comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic and transport models.
The numerical simulation is also being used as a predictive tool to develop the science requirements for this experiment, especially the collection of test conditions and most aspects of the measurement systems. Due to time and g-jitter limitations, little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in the ground based test facilities, and the flight experiment definition will rely on the best effort in the modeling work.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters.

_source.Objectives:
PK-4 is not an apparatus dedicated for specific experiments but rather a laboratory which shall offer the possibility to perform a large variety of experiments with complex plasmas and to react to new developments in this field in a manner as flexible as possible.
The main interest lies in the investigation of the liquid phase and flow phenomena of complex plasmas for which PK-4 is especially suited thanks to a DC-discharge and its geometry (elongated glass tube with a large observational access).


The experiments for PK-4 can be divided into research in three classes of fundamental questions:
1. Microscopic properties of complex plasmas
  This category comprises the charging of the particles, the external forces on the particles (e.g. ion drag), the fundamental interactions between the particles, agglomeration, and particle growth.
2. Macroscopic properties of complex plasmas
  In this category belong hydrodynamics (e.g. viscosity), thermodynamics (e.g. equation of state), and non-equilibriums aspects (e.g. lane formation, self-organisation) of complex plasmas.
3. Generic properties of classical many-body systems
  Complex plasmas are ideal model systems for studying various problems of strongly coupled many-body systems in solid state physics, fluid physics, plasma physics, nano-technology and even nuclear physics because complex plasmas can easily be produced and observed in real time on the microscopic and kinetic level. Hence dynamical processes can be investigated on the level of single particles which is not possible in most systems.

Therefore new insights in the dynamics of those processes can be provided. Typical examples are crystallization and melting, phonons in plasma crystals, dust waves, Mach cones, nozzles, turbulence, and nano-fluidics.
_source.Approach:
The basic experimental protocol starts with an evacuation of the plasma chamber for several hours (a minimum of 20 hours; base pressure: less than 10-3 Pa) to guarantee good plasma conditions, e.g. no striations.

Then neon or argon gas is filled in with a gas flow of typically 2 sccm reaching pressures between 5 and 250 Pa.

Afterwards the plasma is ignited by the high-voltage (about 1000 V) of the DC electrodes corresponding to a DC current of the order of 1 mA and a longitudinal electric field of about 2 V/cm.

Then the micro-particles are injected. They get quickly charged in the plasma and drift from the cathode to the anode with a typical velocity between 1 and 10 cm/s.

In addition, the electric fields from the two RF coils/electrodes or the fast polarity switching can be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to capture and confine them.

Gas flow, modulation of the DC and RF fields, the powerful manipulation laser, the thermal manipulator, and the EM electrode can also be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to accelerate them or to introduce oscillations.

A sketch of the PK-4 experiment is shown in Figure 1. The micro-particles are made visible by illumination with a laser beam, which is widened into a sheet by a cylindrical lens. The scattered light is recorded by one or two CCD cameras (e.g. up to 200 frames per second, with a maximum resolution of about e.g.10 microns/pixel). The light emission (“plasma glow”) from the plasma will be measured using the narrow band IF-filters.

The basic measurements comprise the positions of the particles, their velocities (extracted from the track length of the particles or from their positions in consecutive images), and correlations between the particles. These quantities are determined from the images by using a dedicated IDL program or other methods for image analysis.

At the end of each experiment run the particles will be removed by gas flow before the plasma is switched off in order to avoid the contamination of the glass walls
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: PK-4 enables fundamental investigation of flows and related instabilities, by mimicking molecular mechanisms at a scale which allows for real time in-situ optical observations. This requires on-orbit experiments to be undertaken in order to observe the processes at work, which are obviously disturbed by the influence of gravity on Earth. Even though PK-4 is principally a fundamental experiment, understanding the processes at work and understanding how complex plasmas can be influenced by varying research parameters gives a better understanding of how improvements can be made in areas and industries where plasmas are used. Understanding how dusty plasmas behave in microgravity could shed light on plasma phenomena in space, which could lead to new research methods or improved spacecraft designs.

_source.Proposal Title: Amyloid Fibril Formation in Microgravity: Distinguishing Interfacial and Flow Effects
_source.Objectives:
This campaign centered on four main objectives: (i) engineering the RSD to flight proven hardware, (ii) testing measurement and instrumentation methods aboard the ISS, (iii) studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and (iv) measuring and modeling protein solution rheology.

The primary obective of this investigation is to quantify the effects of flow on fibrillization in the bulk and at interfaces, specifically at the air/water interface. This includes studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and measuring and modeling protein solution rheology. The overall objective is project  to advance the mechanistic description of
fibrillization by determining how shearing flow affects each of the stages of amyloid
formation process − protein unfolding and nuclei formation, growth into protofibrils, and
elongation and intertwining into mature fibrils and fibril growth − without any influence
from solid boundaries.
_source.Approach:
The Ring Shear Drop (RSD) is used to facilitate amyloidogenesis and study flow dynamics without solid wall interactions. It uses surface tension to contain fluids in a microgravity environment. Techniques like Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) are used to measure fluid dynamics and protein interactions. This information was used to create high-fidelity computational models.
Formation and flow of protein aggregates on the surface of the drop will be imaged by the microscope as a function of time. The RSD imaged the surface of a 2.50 cm diameter drop of protein solution with shear imposed by the rotation of one of the two sharp-edged rings (essentially knife edges) that constrain the drop.  A separate measure of the turbidity quantified by the extinction of a light beam through the center of the drop provided an independent signal for fibril formation. A variable degree of shear was imposed on the drop with a negligible contact with solid boundaries. Velocity of the fluid on the surface
of the drop will be determined by standard cross-correlation techniques from images obtained by the microscope. Details regarding sample composition and experimental parameters can be found in RSD Experimental Table.
_source.Hypothesis: The absence of gravity in a microgravity environment will significantly alter the amyloid fibril formation process in proteins.The hypothesis tested was that if protein solutions in microgravity are seeded with fibrils and subject to steady interfacial shear, then amyloidogenesis will occur with the extent of gelation depending on total protein concentration.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Amyloid fibril formation in proteins is of great interest because of its role in diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. For example, the waxy plaque choking off neurons in Alzheimer’s patients consists of the A-beta protein that has formed into amyloid fibrils. The microgravity environment aboard the ISS was utilized to study the biophysics of protein amyloidogenesis. The absence of gravity allows surface tension to provide fluid containment so that wall nucleation and other complications associated with solid containers can be avoided. Flow effects on protein fibrillization was studied at fluid interfaces similar to physiological processes, as all brain tissue consists of interfaces with fluidity, being comprised of cell membranes. The goal is to advance mechanistic descriptions of amyloid fibril formation.

_source.Approach:
The experimental approach was to perform directional solidification experiments with a pure metal, aluminum, doped with low
volume fraction of insoluble particles, ZrO2. These experiments were carried out during the Life and Microgravity Science (LMS) mission on board the space shuttle Columbia. In addition, transparent organic matrices such as succinonitrile and biphenyl doped with polystryrene particles or glass beads were used to observe the interaction between the particle and solidification interface in real time. The experiments with the organic matrices were performed during the United States Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission also on board the space shuttle Columbia. Planar interfaces were produced through appropriate manipulation of the solidification variables, so that a clear pushing/engulfment transition (PET) of the particles could be determined. Both ground and microgravity experiments were conducted.
Recognizing that the interaction between the particle and the solidification front is not completely a steady state process, a dynamic non-steady-state model was developed based on the fact that a particle, initially at rest, must have an accelerated motion in order to reach the steady-state velocity, which is the solidification velocity. To account for the solutal fields in alloys a 2D FDM fixed Cartesian grid numerical model was also developed. The models were validated using benchmark microgravity and terrestrial data.
_source.Hypothesis: During solidification of metal-insoluble particles systems the particles interact with the solidification front. The solutal and thermal field, as well as fluid motion at the solid-liquid interface (SLI) will influence both interface morphology and the particle/interface interaction itself. This investigation hypothesizes that based on the nature of interaction and balance of forces acting on the particle there is a critical SLI velocity below which particles are pushed ahead of the advancing interface, and above which particle engulfment occurs. For planar SLI the critical velocity results from the forces acting on the particle. These forces include particle-SLI interaction force, drag force on the particle, gravitational force, Saffman force, and Magnus force. The last three are strongly affected by the level of gravitational acceleration.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: A fundamental understanding of the phenomena associated with particle/interface interaction during solidification will permit the development of novel techniques for processing of particulate metal matrix composites through melting and solidification. Similar concepts apply to inclusion management in casting alloys. As for most other metallurgical applications it is desired to avoid inclusion segregation at grain boundaries. Results of this research can be extrapolated straightforward to “clean steel” technology. Another interesting application of particle pushing is in the processing of single crystals ceramic where strong flux pinning particles are desired to be homogeneously incorporated in the superconducting crystal. Insights from this investigation can also be applied to the field of cryobiology where the study of the interaction of cells (yeast cells, red blood cells) with ice crystals when freezing aqueous solutions makes it possible to investigate the mechanism of the mechanical destruction of biological structures by ice crystals on freezing biological materials. In addition, this investigation can be extended to the field of frost heaving of soils that can be reduced to the behavior of soil particles (i.e. clay) in a water/ice matrix.

_source.Proposal Title: Dynamical Selection of Three-Dimensional Interfacial Patterns in Directional Solidification
_source.Objectives: The objective of this investigation was to obtain benchmark data on cellular and dendritic growth under diffusive growth conditions. Precise measurements of interface shape, cell/dendrite tip radius, tip composition and tip temperature will be carried out as a function of composition, growth rate and thermal gradient values.  By systematically varying the process parameters in the absence of gravity-induced convection, the range of interface morphologies will be obtained, yielding insight into the underlying principles that govern dynamical pattern selection. Directional solidification experiments conducted in microgravity using transparent organic analogues will provide real time benchmark data to quantitatively determine conditions for the planar to cellular and cell to dendrite transitions and validate a predictive phase field 3D being developed as part of the investigation.
_source.Approach: Experiments were performed within the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI) of the Device for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization (DECLIC) aboard the International Space Station. Homogeneous 3D cylindrical samples in a classical Bridgman setup was processed with various pulling velocities V and temperature gradients G. The transparent succinonitrile (SCN)-0.24wt% camphor alloy was the sample material and it permitted in situ optical imaging of the solid/liquid interface. Experiments were typically initiated from a single crystal growing along the temperature gradient direction. The alloy solidified within a cylindrical crucible with an inner diameter of 10mm. The solid/liquid interface was located within a stable and well-controlled temperature gradient. The crucible was pulled through an axial adiabatic zone, allowing the interface to grow up to 100 mm in length at a controlled velocity. While independently controlling V and  G experienced by the interface, in situ evolution of the solid/liquid interface morphology was imaged and analyzed. 3D phase-field simulations were specifically developed to identify ranges of primary spacings for the formation of the classically observed “fingers” (deep cells) with blunt tips and “needles” with parabolic tips.
_source.Hypothesis: When a planar solid-liquid becomes unstable, under certain growth conditions, complex interactions among perturbed regions can lead to different amplification rates of different wavelengths that determines the final selection of the reorganized pattern. This complex dynamical process selects a small range of wavelengths, from an unstable spectrum of wavelengths, to form a periodic array of cells.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: From the technological viewpoint, the importance of cellular and dendritic microstructures is quite clear since these structures are exhibited in all important commercial solidification techniques. The proposed project will for the first time provide benchmark data for the dynamical evolution of three-dimensional cellular and dendritic patterns that will enable precise modeling of complex commercial processing technologies to give reliable products. The development of a reliable model will allow industries to design new materials and processing conditions that will have a significant impact on the economy in the US, since casting and welding industries are several billion dollars industries. In addition, the fundamental knowledge of pattern formation will allow the development of nano-scale patterns in polymers and electronic materials that will have significant impact on the development of high technology and advanced materials.

_source.Objectives: The objective of the ACE-TR (Ellipsoid) experiment was to image and document the self-assembly of complex 3D structures formed from small elliptical colloidal particles suspended in a fluid. Temperature gradients were varied with the objective to explore the effect of thermophoresis on colloidal crystallization. The goal was to crystallize a metastable colloidal liquid to study how the orientation and periodicity in particle arrangement evolves in different regions of the phase diagram of elliptical colloidal particles. The objective was to understand the effects of gravity on colloidal self-assembly, test predictions of current theories for soft materials, and develop novel techniques that can be applied to combine materials with  different densities in additive manufacturing. The expected outcome has the potential to make novel colloidal materials in a Low-Earth orbit and return them to Earth.
_source.Approach: ACE-TR will view collections of temperature-controlled, fluorescent-core micron-sized colloidal particles. It uses two different sets of ellipsoids, each in their own sample cells. These have aspect ratios of either 1x2.8 or 1x4.5 microns. The particles are small enough that 50 of them could be placed end to end across the width of a fine human hair; yet big enough that the particles and the structures they form can be photographed with visible light of a confocal microscope. The observations will be done using a 3D confocal microscope at the particle level for sufficiently high particle concentrations; in some samples, we will attempt to control the desired concentration by applying a temperature gradient, to see if the particle number density will adjust itself as a function of temperature throughout the sample cell. ImageJ software and internally developed MATLAB functions and scripts were used for processing and quantification of images collected.
_source.Hypothesis: Despite the fundamental and technological importance, the understanding of colloidal crystallization is still elusive. This investigation hypothesizes that there is interrelation between processes driving orientation and periodicity in particle arrangement.  Comparing the outcome of the ACE-T11 (Hard Spheres) and ACE-TR (Ellipsoids) experiments should help elucidate this interrelation. This will enable a better understanding at the particle level of how a disordered arrangement of elliptical particles self-organizes into a 3D ordered structure.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: ACE-TR reveals several fundamental and practical aspects of soft matter science with potential applications on Earth. Self-assembly processes are crucial to making functional materials and devices from small particles. Improved design and assembly of structures fabricated in microgravity may have use in a variety of fields from medicine to opto-electronics on Earth. Ultimately, the ability to design and build functional structures based on colloids will allow new devices for chemical energy, communication, and photonics, including photonic materials to control and manipulate light. The rapidly growing fields of 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on the assembly and sintering of particle aggregates and the preparation of high-density slurries and pastes of different colloidal materials and with different rheological and mechanical properties.  These ellipsoids may  behave like liquid crystals when they self-assemble and their possible defects (hedgehogs) may also be visible.

_source.Proposal Title: Batch 1 Processing of Sample #09 FeCrNi
_source.Objectives:
The objective of this project is to understand phase selection in structural alloys and to investigate the effects of convection on time-dependent nucleation phenomena during rapid solidification from the melt.  The ELFSTONE investigation involves a collaboration with the European Space Agency's (ESA) Thermolab Experiment which focuses on thermophysical properties data measurement of industrial alloys in the liquid phase as a function of temperature. The property values obtained are used to increase the accuracy of numerical modeling of casting and solidification processes of metal alloys.
For access to data relating to the Thermolab Experiment, please consult ESA's HRE Data Archive (hreda.esac.esa.int)
_source.Approach: The samples are processed in the Electromagnetic Levitator (ISS-EML), a facility that has been operational since 2015 and is located in the Columbus module. The investigation is part of Sample Batch 1 - the first of six proposed 18-sample multi-user cartridges uploaded to the ISS.  For the ELFSTONE Sample #09, a ternary FeCrNi analog steel sample, a process cycle is defined as (1) the melting of the sample, (2) the gathering of science data, and (3) the subsequent undercooling and rapid solidification of the sample. The next cycle starts with the re-melting of the sample.  In any particular cycle, stirring may be induced at different levels to study the effect of convection on rapid solidification behavior.  After all cycles are complete, final microstructure is preserved for return to earth.
_source.Hypothesis: The experimental hypothesis was that melt convection would significantly decrease the nucleation kinetics for transformation of metastable ferrite to stable austenite in ferrous structural steel alloys. The was successfully observed.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The value of this research is that the results have application to the design of industrial welding, spray forming, and casting operations for a commercially important class of structural materials. In addition, this research addresses fundamental issues relating to rapid solidification behavior, metastable phase selection, and analysis of the processes governing microstructural evolution. Experiments focus on the use of convection as a processing control parameter.

_source.Proposal Title: Flame Design: A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames
_source.Objectives:
The primary objectives of this flight experiment are:
A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames.
B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames.
C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames.
_source.Approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station. Consider a broad range of reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
_source.Hypothesis:
1. Soot formation requires a region where local C/O ratio and T exceed their critical values, and where strain rate is sufficiently low.
2. Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K.
3. Steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.

_source.Title: Microheater Array Boiling Experiment
_source.Keywords: MABE     microscale heater array     boiling     bubble dynamics
_source.Objectives:
1. To characterize the boiling curve in a very low g-jitter environment: The experiment aims to determine the boiling curve in a microgravity environment with minimal gravitational disturbances (g-jitter). This objective is driven by the understanding that g-jitter can significantly influence bubble dynamics and, consequently, the heat transfer process. By minimizing g-jitter, the researchers hope to obtain a clearer picture of boiling behavior in a true microgravity environment.

2. To understand the parameters governing the size of the primary bubble and develop a predictive model for it: A key objective is to identify the factors that determine the size of the primary bubble in microgravity. These parameters could include heater size, nucleation site density, subcooling, gravity level, fluid properties, superheated layer thickness, wall superheat, and surface tension. By understanding these parameters, the researchers aim to develop a model that can accurately predict the primary bubble size under different conditions.

3. To investigate the mechanism of critical heat flux (CHF) in microgravity and its relationship to the primary bubble: The research aims to elucidate how CHF occurs in microgravity and to determine its relationship to the size and behavior of the primary bubble. CHF is a critical parameter in boiling, representing the maximum heat flux that can be transferred from a surface before a transition to film boiling occurs. Understanding the factors influencing CHF in microgravity is essential for the safe and efficient operation of space-based thermal systems.

4. To determine the effect of heater size on the formation of the primary bubble and its impact on the boiling curve: MABE investigates the influence of heater size on boiling behavior. Two different heater array sizes are used, allowing the researchers to compare how heater size affects the formation of the primary bubble, the occurrence of dryout, and the shape of the boiling curve in microgravity.
_source.Approach:
MABE utilizes a multi-pronged approach to achieve its research objectives. The experiment combines a carefully designed experimental setup with a comprehensive data analysis strategy. Here's a breakdown of the key elements of the investigation approach:

Experimental Setup:

Microscale heater array: The experiment utilizes an array of 96 individually controlled platinum resistance heaters deposited on a quartz substrate.

Constant temperature control: Each heater is maintained at a constant temperature, allowing for accurate quantification of substrate heat conduction and reducing the risk of heater burnout.

Variable experimental conditions: The experiment manipulates key parameters such as bulk liquid subcooling, pressure, and heater size to study their influence on boiling.

Multiple gravity levels: The experiment is designed to allow data acquisition in Earth gravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, and microgravity, enabling a comprehensive comparison of boiling behavior across different gravitational environments.

High-speed video imaging: A high-speed digital camera captures images of the boiling process beneath the heater array, providing valuable insights into bubble dynamics.

Interferometry: The experiment employs interferometry to measure temperature profiles around the vapor bubble, providing additional data for analysis.

Data Acquisition and Analysis:

Data Acquisition: Data is collected at a high frequency, capturing the instantaneous power dissipated by each heater, bulk fluid temperature, pressure, and acceleration.

Data Processing: Raw data is converted into engineering units, synchronized, and analyzed to generate boiling curves, heat transfer maps, and other relevant data visualizations.

Correlation with video and interferometry data: The heat transfer data is correlated with visual observations from the high-speed video and interferometry data to gain a deeper understanding of bubble behavior and heat transfer mechanisms.

Analytical and Numerical Modeling: The experiment employs analytical and numerical models to simulate the boiling process and validate the experimental findings.

Ground-Based Testing and Validation:

Preliminary Engineering Model: A preliminary engineering model of the experiment is developed and tested on the KC-135 aircraft, providing essential validation of the design and data acquisition procedures.

Calibration and Validation: The heater array is calibrated on the ground and recalibrated in flight to ensure accurate measurements.

This investigation approach combines a sophisticated experimental setup with rigorous data analysis and modeling to provide a comprehensive understanding of boiling in microgravity.
_source.Hypothesis: This study will test three central hypotheses: (1) Bubble coalescence dominates heat transfer in microgravity, creating a large primary bubble that induces local dryout; (2) A transition between buoyancy-dominated and surface-tension-dominated boiling regimes occurs depending on the interplay between the heater size and the gravitational acceleration; (3) Heat transfer in the surface-tension-dominated regime shows minimal dependence on gravitational acceleration.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: In microgravity, a bubble can cover an entire heater array instead of just a small area, resulting in burnout of components if local hot spots are present. The increased spatial resolution of these measurements will enable the extent of the dry spot to be measured along with the heat transfer from the liquid surrounding the dry spot. This technique can be applied to other areas including spray cooling, turbulence measurements and flow boiling. The proposed research has shown that transient conduction is the dominant heat transfer mechanism in boiling of refrigerants-like fluids. This research will provide insight into creating more efficient cooling systems on Earth.
