_source.Title: Characterization of Biofilm Formation, Growth and Gene Expression on Different Materials and Environmental Conditions in Microgravity
_source.Keywords: Transcriptomics     Microorganisms     Microbiology     Biofilms     Experimental Design     Gene-Expression     SpaceBio
_source.Proposal Title: Characterization of Biofilm Formation, Growth and Gene Expression on Different Materials and Environmental Conditions in Microgravity
_source.Objectives: 1. To use microbial strains that are relevant to human spaceflight, and nosocomial infections that have also occurred in spaceflight, and substrata materials that are relevant to (i) spacecraft structures and surfaces, (ii) life support systems, (iii) space biology research hardware, and (iv) medical instrumentation. We are meeting this objective by the use of the same fungal strain that was isolated from a bio-damaged Mir window (Penicillium rubens), and an uropathogenic bacterial strain (Pseudomonas aeruginosa).  2. To culture the selected microbial strains in a way that enables biofilm formation, during an up- to-6-month experiment. To achieve this goal, we used BioServe’s already spaceflight- proven hardware and conducted preliminary testing during the first year of the experiment. 3. To quantify potential changes on biofilm mass, thickness, and overall morphology (including the formation of the “column-and-canopy structures) on the spaceflight cultures with respect to matched ground controls. This was achieved by acquiring post-flight (samples fixed in paraformaldehyde) morphological data through confocal laser scanning microscopy. 4. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind the observed morphological changes. This was done with the bacterial samples by acquiring post-flight transcriptomic data (samples fixed with RNA Later II) and conducting differential gene expression analyses between spaceflight cultures and matched ground controls. 5. To assess differential expression of genes associated with conferring microbes with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance. This was done through RNA Sequencing and comparative gene analysis. 6. To determine physical mechanisms of material/microorganisms interaction in biofilms and their associated molecular basis. The morphological and transcriptomic data was utilized to identify potential correlation in between the differential gene expression and altered material/microorganism interaction in space, with respect to matched ground controls. Different topographic structures were assessed to provide further insight into this aspect (topographical patters with periodicities, same size, as the microbial size).
_source.Approach:
The Space Biofilms project, performed at the International Space Station, contributes to the understanding of microbial communities in space by characterizing the morphology and gene expression of bacterial and fungal biofilms formed in microgravity with respect to ground controls. The project has two big branches, the bacterial and the fungal side. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was used as model organism for the bacterial side and both morphology and transcriptomic (selected samples) studies were performed with bacterial samples, while Penicillium rubens was used as model organism for the fungal side and a morphology study was performed for fungal samples. Bacterial biofilm formation was characterized at one, two, and three days of incubation (37°C) over six different materials: stainless steel 316, passivated stainless steel 316, a lubricant impregnated surface (LIS), catheter grade silicone with and without a linear microtopography, and cellulose membrane. Fungal biofilm formation (mold) was characterized at 10, 15, and 20 days of incubation (25°C) over seven different materials: stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy (Al6061), titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V), quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”.
Bacterial samples: 144 flight and 144 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms bacterial experiment. The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (1, 2, and 3 days), six material-media combinations (LBK media was used for samples grown over SS316, pSS316, and LIS; while mAUMg-hi Pi media was used for samples grown over cellulose, silicone, and silicone DLIP), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (four). To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) and eight FPAs were integrated into a Group Activation Pack (GAP). Once in microgravity, samples were activated by introducing the bacterial inoculum into the sterile medium and placing the samples at 37°C for the corresponding incubation time. After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples). The morphology samples were stained (one dye for lipids and one dye for nucleic acids) and imaged with a confocal microscope. The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage. The transcriptomic samples had their RNA extracted and sequenced. The resulting transcriptomic data files (fastq files) were processed and used for gene expression analysis using DeSeq2.
For more information on the bacterial sample preparation see section 4, and for information about the experiment performance in space see section 5 of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actaastro.2022.07.015 For more information on the bacterial morphology and transcriptomic analyses see the Methods section of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41526-023-00316-w
Fungal samples: 288 flight and 288 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms fungal experiment. The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (10, 15, and 20 days), seven material substratum (stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy Al6061, titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V, quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (6-12 depending on the specific set). To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a well of a 24-well plate and sealed with a gas permeable membrane. Additionally, four 24-well plates were integrated into a Plate Habitat (PHAB). Once in microgravity, samples were activated by wetting pads inside the PHAB to increase the environment humidity and by placing the samples at 25°C for the corresponding incubation time. After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples)*. *The transcriptomic samples were not analyzed as part of this project. The morphology samples were stained (one dye for chitin and one dye for extracellular matrix proteins) and imaged with a confocal microscope. The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage.
For more information on the bacterial sample preparation, the experiment performance in space, and the fungal morphology analyses see section 2 of the following paper:- https://doi.org/10.3390/life13041001
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that, in comparison to matched ground controls: a) Biofilm mass and thickness in microgravity will be increased for all bacterial and fungal species, growth medium, and substratum material; b) Gene expression will vary as a function of growth medium, substratum material, and gravitational regime; c) A systematic increase in expression of the genes that confer microorganisms with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance will be observed in space (becoming more pronounced with time in space); and d) The formation of the “column-and- canopy” bacterial biofilm architecture and the material/microorganism interaction mechanisms in space will vary from one microbial species and material to the other, and will be associated with the differential expression of specific genes.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This project is relevant to the space program and the “Biophysics – Biomaterials” emphasis of this NRA as it investigates biofilm formation (which can increase the risk of astronaut infection and equipment failure) on spacecraft-relevant materials. This work is relevant to the Space Biology Program and the Human Research Roadmap as it utilizes human pathology-associated bacterial species (uropathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa), growth media (e.g. modified artificial urine media), and materials (e.g. silicone from catheters).The knowledge produced may help address Gaps Micro-01, -02, -03, and -04 by characterizing bacterial and fungal responses to spaceflight, by interrogating the expression of genes associated with drug resistance, and by elucidating the governing mechanisms behind the observed phenomena. Furthermore, due to our proposed approach, the knowledge derived from this project may be translatable to biofilm-associated illnesses on Earth.

_source.Title: Electrically Driven Liquid Film Flow Boiling in the Absence of Gravity
_source.Keywords: EHD     electric conduction     electric fields     boiling     Reduced Gravity     Electrodrodynamics     dielectrophoresis     critical heat flux     heat transfer     Presence of Gravity
_source.Proposal Title: Electrically Driven Liquid Film Flow Boiling: A Two-Phase Heat Transport Device Driven by Electric Conduction and Dielectrophoretic Mechanisms
_source.Objectives:
a-Provide fundamental understanding of the combined electrically driven (based on EHD conduction phenomenon) liquid film flow and dielectroporetic vapor extraction mechanism in the presence of phase change (liquid to vapor) in the absence of gravity.

b-Provide a phenomenological foundation for the future development of electric field based two phase thermal management systems, leveraging EHD engineering advantages to develop systems of arbitrary mass flow requirements and geometries.
_source.Approach: As vapor bubbles cover the surface and grow or coalesce, the modes of heat transfer will be limited to conduction and possibly radiation. To avoid this and to enable boiling to take place, EHD-driven liquid film will be fed from the condenser section towards the heater. The inertia of liquid film flow along with DEP extraction force will repel vapor bubbles that have formed on the heater surface. In order to study the competing effects of flow inertia/DEP extraction force vs. bubble behavior in zero gravity, one needs to understand EHD generated liquid film flow and the DEP mechanism. The flow inertia is a function of applied EHD potential, electrode design, liquid film thickness and working fluid properties. The DEP extraction force is also a function of its corresponding electrode design, the spacing between its electrode and heated surface, and the applied potential for a given working fluid. Thus, the controlling parameters for this study are applied EHD conduction pumping potential, applied DEP potential, heat flux, and liquid film height for the selected working fluid and electrode designs.  The electrode designs for EHD conduction pumping and DEP mechanism are based on our previous numerical and experimental work. Therefore, the electrode dimensions, design or distance from the heater surface will not need to be varied during this study.
_source.Hypothesis: Boiling is not acceptable in the absence of gravity unless the generated vapor bubbles can be expelled from the boiling surface and fresh liquid can be pumped onto the hot surface through some mechanism. EHD conduction pumping has the capability of pumping thin liquid films toward the heat source where the boiling takes place, with sufficient inertia to begin expelling bubbles from the heated surface at low heat fluxes. Furthermore, applying an EHD Dielectrophoretic (DEP) extraction force near the boiling surface guarantees the repulsion of vapor bubbles away from the heated surface even at high heat fluxes. Finally, the combined EHD driven liquid film flow boiling and DEP extraction force are expected to sustain and enhance the critical heat flux in the absence of gravity. Combining EHD conduction and DEP effects is therefore critical to the success of the ISS experiment.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This multi-physics proposal will provide basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e., dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity. The electrically driven liquid film flow boiling data aboard ISS will determine the critical heat flux, onset of boiling, absence of hysteresis, and bubble characteristics in the absence of gravity.There are a number of potential terrestrial and space applications for this electrohydrodynamic (EHD) driven two-phase heat transport device in all scales (from macro-scale to truly micro-scales). For example, this device can be used to effectively remove heat from electronics in micro- and zero-gravity environment for NASA's future space stations and long term missions. It can also be used in satellites (e.g., embedded system into satellite's multi-functional structure).Terrestrially, it can be used in high intensity electronics cooling as well as in various phase change devices. To achieve these applications, the basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e.,dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity is needed.

_source.Proposal Title: Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity
_source.Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
_source.Approach:
The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .
The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows:
  1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests.
  2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm)
  3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size).
  4. Perform a droplet combustion test.
  5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed).
  6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction).
  7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction.
  8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite.

There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure  involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI . For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow.  In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed).

The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity. Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.
_source.Hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

_source.Proposal Title: Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment
_source.Objectives: The primary objective of the microgravity dendritic growth experiment was to measure definitively the kinetics and morphology of dendritic growth, and to account for the effects of natural convection. The experimental objective was to use a single,clearly defined experimental parameter, namely, the supercooling, to fully determine the resulting steady-state dendritic growth velocity, V, and tip radius R. Designated the IDGE, the first flight, manifested on the second United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-2) mission, was launched and operated on the STS-62 on March 4-18, 1994. This IDGE investigation met the objective of acquiring accurate dendritic growth speed and morphology data under diffusion-controlled conditions, while greatly reducing buoyancy-induced convective heat transport through the reduction of gravity. The microgravity environment broadened this range of supercooling and permitted for the first time a critical assessment of both the heat transport theory and the interfacial kinetics behavior.
_source.Approach:
The approach was to observe and image dendritic growth as a function of undercooling such that dendritic tip velocities and radii could both be accurately measured and used as a critical test of theory. Succinonitrile (SCN), transparent when molten, was used as a model metal analog system for studying dendritic growth since it solidifies like the body centered cubic (BCC) ferrous metal alloys, i.e., with an atomically ''rough'' solid-liquid interface. In addition, SCN displays convenient properties for solidification experiments, such as a low melting temperature (58.08 °C), optical transparency, and the potential for accurate characterization of its thermophysical properties. Dendritic growth is initiated inside the experimental chamber by energizing thermoelectric coolers attached to one end a thin capillary injector tube called the stinger. The other end of the stinger, where the dendrite emerges in the center of the chamber, is notched, much like the tip of a fountain pen. This helps isolate the leading dendrite and reduces the time needed until the leading dendrite is isothermal and has achieved steady state.
The IDGE flight experiment was divided into 60 operational cycles. The first cycle, the warm-up cycle, consists of bringing the system up to the operational temperature where all system components are checked and initialized. The second cycle measured the liquidus temperature of the SCN as a calibration point from which all subsequent supercoolings are measured. The remaining cycles were dendritic growth cycles where dendrites are grown and photographed at varying supercoolings. For each dendritic growth cycle, the experiment obtained a time series of stereo-pairs of 35-mm photographic images, low-resolution, binary, digitized electronic images and various data streams characterizing the dendrite's growth conditions during the cycle. For each image pair, either 35-mm film negative or digitized image, we measured the position of the dendrite tip, and the associated time that the image was recorded. The dendritic velocity was determined by calculating the slope of the displacement-time curve from the steady-state regime of the growth cycle. The velocity is then adjusted by appropriate stereographic and magnification factors. This procedure yields a set of dendrite velocity measurements accurate to about ± 2 percent.
_source.Hypothesis: The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second  crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in  the melt, or both.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help  design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance. Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

_source.Objectives: The main objective of the DSI-R investigation was to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions. This investigation particularly focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity and study the potential for the formation of an intermediate multiplet pattern. The dynamics and stability of cellular and dendritic growth patterns, and the relationship between the tip geometry and growth pattern were also to be investigated as well. This intent of this investigation was to directly address outstanding issues that remain open in the understanding of complex dendritic microstructures.
_source.Approach: The DSI-R investigation utilized a Bridgman type furnace and an experimental cartridge containing the organic transparent alloy of succinonitrile (SCN) - camphor. The nominal concentration was 0.46 wt% camphor. A single crystalline solid seed with a 100 direction parallel to the pulling axial direction is kept unmelted during all experiments.  Solidification is performed by pulling the experimental cartridge containing the alloy inside a thermal gradient G at a pulling rate V. The G and V were the primary variable for each experimental run. Images obtained by the direct axial observation, providing top-view interface images, and transverse observations, providing side-view interface images, were analyzed.
_source.Hypothesis:
Bridgman solidification of transparent binary alloys in a diffusion controlled growth regime can yield benchmark data required for establishing the detailed dynamics of interface pattern selection.

The ''SPAtiotemporal evolution of three-dimensional DEndritic array Structures'' (SPADES) investigation conducted during the reflight of the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI-R) campaign targeted the columnar dendritic growth regime to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions.

SPADES focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity.

The “Effects of Curvature and Unsteady Dynamics on Alloy Solidification Patterns” (CUSP) investigation extended the DSIP and SPADES project into a new direction that addressed the critical effects of the macroscopic curvature of the solidification front and the unsteady dynamics that occurs in response to changes of growth conditions or that is associated with side-branching.

A weak macroscopic interface curvature can have a major effect on both the array pattern evolution and grain structure. The convex and concave interfaces lead to a continuous increase and decrease  of the average primary spacing, respectively, and it only attains a stationary value for a flat interface.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: By providing a reduced gravity environment where fluid convection is suppressed, space enables the direct experimental observation of the solid-liquid interface dynamics during the solidification process under long-duration and purely diffusive conditions. The acquired benchmark data will make it uniquely possible to critically test computational models of alloy microstructures by quantitative comparisons of modeling predictions and experimental observations, thereby contributing to the development of Integrated Computational Materials and Engineering (ICME) tools for both space and earth applications. Those tools are expected to “shorten development time, optimize designs and reduce costs relative to more traditional strategies involving building prototypes, testing and redesigning philosophies. In addition, understanding alloy solidification in the microgravity environment of space is important to improve in-space processing (manufacturing, joining, and welding) of structural materials that will be used for future space exploration.

_source.Objectives:
The primary objective of this investigation was to understand why protein crystallization experiments in microgravity have generated unexpectedly low or high numbers of crystals. Each outcome may cause experiments designed to obtain a small number of well-separated crystals to fail.

The objective of the proposed investigations is to explore the effects of a hitherto unstudied factor for the nucleation of protein crystals: solution shear flow. Besides providing a novel tool for nucleation control for protein crystallization experiments, the correlation between solution flows and protein crystal nucleation, to be tested in the proposed investigation, will shed light on one of the major mysteries of current space biophysics: the finding that in many cases the number of crystals nucleated in microgravity was greater or smaller than those nucleated on earth.
_source.Approach: Three cassettes containing five capillaries each were loaded with one of three proteins; (1) Lysozyme, (2) p53, and (3) hnRNPA-LC. The observation of these protein clusters were observed with a newly developed technique, called differential dynamic microscopy (DDM). DDM improves a recent method used to study and quantify the dynamics of sub-micrometer particles in solutions from fluctuations in intensity in optical micrographs. All samples were frozen to a temperature of -80C before flight to the ISS. The proteins were thawed and observed over several weeks in the ISS LMM module where they were filmed and photographed. Sample details and experimental parameters are summarized in LMMBio2_Experimental Table in the science document section.
_source.Hypothesis:
Hypothesis: The behavior of dense liquid clusters at different rates of convection will have a profound effect on crystal growth.

The main hypothesis underlying the proposed investigations consists of two parts:
1. The existence of nucleation precursors and the correlation between their properties and the nucleation rate can be used to control protein crystal nucleation via solution flow.
2. Enhancement or suppression of nucleation via solution flow, i.e., independently of solution supersaturation, can be used to achieve higher perfection of the grown crystals.
3. A very small fraction of the protein exists in a dense liquid phase in the form of Brownian particles, each a cluster of roughly 105 protein molecules undergoing liquid-like dynamics.
4. Crystal nucleation occurs when a small, ordered domain forms within the highly concentrated liquid-state environment of one of these particles.

_source.Objectives: Following the first IDGE flight on USMP-2, the second fight of lDGE took place on USMP-3 in February and March of 1996. The scientific objectives of the second flight of the IDGE was to: characterize the three-dimensional shape of a dendrite tip; accumulate a dense data set on dendritic velocities and radii in the diffusion-limited infinite boundary regime; and to form dendritic velocity data sets to clarify issues in the literature about whether convection or near-field boundary conditions affect the dendritic growth measurements in microgravity in the lower supercooling range.
_source.Approach: The sample material and temperature controls were identical to the USMP-2 investigation. In addition to the high-resolution film data collected after the shuttle landed, growth velocities were measured in near-real time by downlinked, binary CCD images. Many growths were measured from CCD images alone and these steady-state velocity measurements were accurate to 2%.
_source.Hypothesis: The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second  crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in  the melt, or both. Aside from the original hypothesis for USMP-2, the USMP-3 also tested the hypothesis that both the magnitude of the microgravity level and the growth angle with respect to the quasi-static microgravity vector would affect the growth velocity. With additional and sufficient data from USMP-3 it was anticipated to construct a three-dimensional reconstruction of the non-parabolic, non-body-of-revolution dendritic tip shape.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help  design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance. Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

_source.Objectives: In this study, the compositions start with W-Ni-Cu-Mn powder mixtures. The solid-liquid ratio is adjusted via changes in the tungsten content from 70 to 90 wt %. Most of the tungsten remains solid during sintering. The liquid is formed from melting the mechanically alloyed Ni-Cu-Mn additive. The liquid dissolves up to 28 wt % tungsten at the sintering temperature, giving the desired semisolid system. In these experiments, changes are also made to the Ni:Cu ratio from 3:2 to 2:3 to slightly adjust the tungsten solubility. Seven cartridges with seven samples each are processed in microgravity. One cartridge is heated to the temperature where first significant densification occurs on Earth, 1180°C, and five of the cartridges are processed for progressively longer times at 1210°C. A seventh cartridge is for backup in case of an aborted run, otherwise it provides a replicate at 34 min at 1210°C. An early part of this research focused on developing a W-Ni-Cu-Mn alloy to allow lower sintering temperatures to accommodate downgraded furnace peak temperatures. The new alloys are tested using ground proof runs to gather ground data. Those results are contrasted with the microgravity data. Extensive testing is documented to show the experimental platform; tests involved thermal overload, vibration, equipment proofing, evaporation, transient runaway, and temperature verification trials. An early failure in the quartz ampoule led to redesign. Subsequent ground runs were conducted without failure. This report emphasizes the development of the experiments and details the densification and distortion data, and provides microstructure data. Modeling ideas were established early and awaited samples for verification. Much effort was directed to developing a time sequence whereby modeling data would be available for rheological variables associated with the solid-liquid-pore structures existing during sintering, namely extraction of the viscosity and strength variations during the 60 min of isothermal hold. The model is implemented in finite element analysis where stress on the sintering body is assessed using variations in the composition, component size, and gravity.
_source.Approach: The idea of removing distortion during liquid phase sintering has much appeal. Loss of dimensional precision during sintering is a common industrial problem. Forming technologies allow for precise green bodies (green is the term adopted to indicate the component after forming, but prior to sintering).  The body force due to gravity acts in the vertical direction and increases with height and density. In these trials, components of 12 mm in height are processed and analyzed for features such as density, dimensional variation (distortion), microstructure, grain size distribution, and pore agglomeration after return to Earth. Gravity normally produces sufficient substrate friction to locally resist shrinkage during sintering, giving an elephant foot geometry. Microgravity trails examine if densification is possible without distortion, the benefit being net-shape processing. For this research on gravity effects on distortion and densification during liquid phase sintering, the two primary metrics are nonuniform dimensional change and the elimination of pores. Along these lines, isotropic right circular cylinders are fabricated for sintering. Both the initial and sintered dimensions are measured over several locations to quantify densification (and shrinkage) and distortion. Densification is measured using dimensional shrinkage (up to 15 %), relying on the change in porosity divided by the initial porosity (37 %). The samples are initially 63 % dense. Distortion is calculated using multiple dimensional measurements over closely spaced locations and is expressed as the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by the mean size). For microstructure assessment to help explain the behavior, the samples are sectioned, mounted, and polished. Optical microscopy, quantitative microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive analysis of X-rays provide information on the microstructure, especially the pore and grain structure. Quantitative microstructure data include grain size, pore size, connectivity, and distributions for these features. The results are compared to models to validate constitutive laws. In prior research microgravity resulted in large pores, extensive distortion, and a low grain connectivity microstructure with smaller grains.
_source.Hypothesis: The idea of removing distortion during liquid phase sintering has much appeal. Loss of dimensional precision during sintering is a common industrial problem. Forming technologies allow for precise green bodies (green is the term adopted to indicate the component after forming, but prior to sintering). The body force due to gravity acts in the vertical direction and increases with height and density. The distortion problem is most evident in structures with protrusions and unsupported or cantilever features. Accordingly, for some liquid phase sintered components a majority of the production expense is in correcting dimensional issues after sintering, by use of coining, straightening, grinding, or machining. Many powder metallurgy components start with a green density of just 60 % of theoretical. Shaping is possible using a variety of options - die pressing, injection molding, warm extrusion, cold isostatic pressing, or slurry casting. High performance demands a high sintered density, often from 98 to 100 %. The change from 60 to 98 % density comes with about 15 % shrinkage in each dimension. However, as the component height increases gravity induces nonuniform shrinkage. The friction force at the component bottom increases. This friction force resists densification on the bottom surface, resulting in nonuniform dimensions, effectively distorting the green body. The economic attraction for sintering technologies is the delivery of net-shapes, avoiding post-sintering machining if possible. Unfortunately, it is easy to lose dimensional control, necessitating secondary operations that add greatly to the fabrication expense. In the ideal, tooling design would anticipate sintering shrinkage, even nonuniform shrinkage, enabling sintering to directly deliver final size. This would be possible with computer tools to design the tooling in anticipation of shrinkage and distortion. Our initial conjecture suggested that liquid phase sintering in microgravity would remove distortion, since shrinkage and microstructure should be uniform.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Sintering is a heat treatment applied to powders with the intent of bonding the particles into a solid structure. It is widely applied to forming complex shapes for automotive, computer, metal cutting, oil and gas drilling, hand tools, firearms, and hardware. Tools is designed to shape the powder into a shape that is oversized to allow for shrinkage. With sufficiently high temperature, heat induces atomic motion and repositioning of solid to form bonds between the particles that strengthen the body. Usually that occurs via diffusion along interfaces such as grain boundary liquid films. In industrial production, the powder is shaped prior to sintering, such as by die compaction or injection molding, with subsequent sintering to produce a complex shape. Accordingly, sintering is frequently applied to high performance materials and is applied in practice over a wide range of products and industries from bricks to rocket engines. It is especially useful for high temperature materials, such as the refractory metals, including tungsten. If densification can be acheived without distortion, considerable expense is avoided by net-shape fabrication. In this sense, tremendous industrial benefit is possible using liquid phase sintering with densifcation but no distortion. In the US sintering technologies are responsible for about 60 kg of each automobile, and dozens of parts in each computer and cell phone. Liquid phase sintering is a desirable option, where in an alloy some liquid forms during the heating cycle (between the liquidus and solidus temperatures for the alloy). The idea of liquid phase sintering gained significance attention during the 1920s as a means to consolidate hard powders, such as cemented carbides (WC-Co), into high performance engineering structures, such as metal cutting tools, wire drawing dies, and oil-less bearings. The tungsten heavy alloys emerged at the same time. It is the latter system selected to demonstrate processing gains or losses associated with gravity.

_source.Proposal Title: Effect of Convection on Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition in Alloy Solidification
_source.Objectives: The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the columnar-to-equiaxed grain structure transition (CET) in solidification of metal alloys. By performing solidification experiments both on earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of gravity-driven melt convection and sedimentation/floatation of unattached dendrite fragments and equiaxed crystals on the CET will be examined. The origin of equiaxed grains in non-refined alloys is of particular interest in the proposed experiments. The benchmark data from these experiments can be used to test theoretical models and computer simulations.
_source.Approach: Experiments were conducted in the Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnace to investigate the CET for stationary samples without an imposed temperature gradient. Most experiments with aluminum-copper (Al-Cu) alloys, namely, Al-4wt%Cu, Al-10wt%Cu and Al-18wt%Cu alloys. The reason is that Al-Cu alloys are better suited for the duplicate ground-based experiments. If solidified upward (low temperature at the bottom, high at the top), thermosolutal natural convection of the melt will generally be minimized. The sedimentation or floatation of dendrite fragments and small equiaxed grains can be controlled by the solute concentration. For smaller solute concentrations, the solid is heavier than the melt and will sediment, while for higher solute concentrations the solid is lighter and will float. Hence, dendrite fragments and equiaxed grains in the Al-18wt%Cu alloy will float upwards ahead of the columnar front, and a CET can be expected. On the other hand, for the Al-4wt%Cu alloy, the fragments will sediment and remain between the primary columnar trunks, and a CET may not occur. For Al-10wt%Cu alloys, the solid is approximately neutrally buoyant in the melt.  An additional experiment with an unrefined Al-7wt%Si alloy was also conducted. No grain refiner was used. In all proposed CET experiments, the samples were first fully melted and then solidified by decreasing the temperature of the SUBSA furnace at a controlled rate. The samples were not moved, and no temperature gradient were explicitly imposed. Corresponding flight and terrestrial experiments were conducted. Samples were analyzed by measuring the grain structure and any macrosegregation.
_source.Hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of this investigation is that fragmentation of columnar dendrites can lead to a CET in non-grain-refined alloys. The secondary dendrite arms that detach from the primary columnar trunks are a potent source of new (equiaxed) grains. However, for a CET to occur the growth of the primary columnar trunks must be blocked by equiaxed grains. This can only be accomplished if the secondary dendrite fragments are transported to the columnar front, rather than remain between the primary columnar trunks. Due to natural convection of the melt and sedimentation or floatation of the fragments, such transport can be expected to readily occur in the gravitational field of earth. In the absence of gravity, it is not clear if fragmentation alone, without fragment transport, is sufficient to cause a CET.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The CET refers to the transition between the elongated grains in the outer portions of a casting and the more rounded grains in the center. Understanding this transition is fundamental to determining what type of grain structure forms in castings of most metal alloys (steel, aluminum, copper, etc.). Often, a fully equiaxed structure is preferred, but the fully columnar structures of many turbine blades are an important exception. In addition to its high practical significance, the CET represents a “holy grail” in the area of modeling and simulation of casting. This is because in order to realistically predict the CET, almost every physical phenomenon at every length scale must be taken into account simultaneously. This investigation will not only provide an improved understanding of the CET, but also models and computer simulations of the grain structure formation in metal castings that can be used by industry to better industry to better understand and optimize their casting processes.

_source.Objectives: Following the first and second IDGE flight on USMP-2 and USMP-3, the third and final IDGE flight (USMP-4) was launched on STS-87, in November of 1997. The last flight employed  pivalic acid (PVA)—a face centered cubic (FCC) organic plastic crystal that solidifies analogous to many non–ferrous metals unlike SCN that solidifies similar to BCC ferrous metal alloys. In comparison to SCN, PVA exhibits a large anisotropy of its solid–melt interfacial energy. The primary objective was to investigate if the anisotropy of solid-melt interfacial energy is indeed a key physical parameter in the subtle selection process of dendritic operating states.
_source.Approach: The experimental approach was similar to USMP-3 and USMP-4 with the exception that PVA was utilized as the sample material to quantify growth velocity as a function of undercooling. In addition, the spacing between nearest neighbors were also quantified during this USMP-4 investigation.
_source.Hypothesis: The hypothesis of the IDGE investigations is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second  crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in  the melt, or both. Aside from the original hypothesis for USMP-2, the USMP-3 also tested the hypothesis that both the magnitude of the microgravity level and the growth angle with respect to the quasi-static microgravity vector would affect the growth velocity. With additional and sufficient data from USMP-3 it was anticipated to construct a three-dimensional reconstruction of the non-parabolic, non-body-of-revolution dendritic tip shape. For the final USMP-4 investigation the use PVA was to test the hypothesis if interfacial anisotropy has any significant effect on growth velocity and if there exist a minimum nearest neighbor distance below which the growth velocity begins to decrease due to overlapping of thermal fields.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help  design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance. Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

_source.Proposal Title: The Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity
_source.Objectives:
The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
  1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
  2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
  3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
  4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
  5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.
  6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.
_source.Approach:
The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes  elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside. This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view. If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted. A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time.

The overall investigation approach can be summarized as:
  1. Test parameters are determined, including pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, and humidity.
  2. Fill the combustion chamber with the selected gas mixtures.
  3. Deploy the droplet(s) carefully controlling the droplet diameter.
  4. Allow the droplet to stabilize in the microgravity environment.
  5. Ignite the droplet in a uniform and controlled fashion.
  6. Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography.
  7. Monitor and adjust experimental conditions as needed.
  8. Analyze data.

The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.
_source.Hypothesis: Fairly sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion have been developed in the last decade where the key contribution is the inclusion of full Navier-Stokes equations for the gas-phase flow field. However, due to the inherent complexity of the problem, varying degrees of approximations have been made in treating the chemistry, radiation, and the coupling between the gas and liquid phases. The validity of the assumptions or the hypothesis used in these simulation have not been confirmed by using benchmark data. By conducting these experiments in a microgravity environment, the effects of buoyancy are minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutalcapillary stresses allowing for a clear observation of the fundamental combustion processes,  The present FLEX-2 experiments using bi-component mixtures. In addition, the microgravity environment allows study of such phenomena as the transitions between radiative and diffusive extension of the flame. The primary goal of the flight experiments is to provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions that could be used to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector. Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to:

  1) More sustainable energy production.
  2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions.
  3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels).
  4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 4
_source.Keywords: Colloidal Glasses     Crystalline Order     Glass Transition     Microgravity
_source.Proposal Title: Low Volume Fraction Entropically Driven Colloidal Assembly
_source.Objectives:
Original Objective: The ACE-T4 experiments were designed to explore the disorder-induced transformation between a crystal and a glass. The experiments introduced disorder by added colloidal dopants into the samples; these dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered solids (polycrystalline) and glasses with novel mechanical properties. The experiments varied the concentration and character of particle dopants in three-dimensional colloidal crystals and employed direct visualization of an evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity to derive fundamental insight into the nature of the transition and the glasses formed.

Revised Objective: Before the ACE-T4 experiment on the International Space Station (ISS) was conducted, the master hard disk controlling the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) failed and delayed starting this experiment by many months. This extended delay had a detrimental effect on the samples that  resulted in the gelation of the samples before the experiment began. The originally planned experiments were no longer possible due to gelation, but the ACE-T4 experiment based on the changed samples (gels) provided qualitatively different insights into the behavior of 3D colloidal gels over a range of temperatures and temperature gradients. Some effects were visible with LMM and provide an opportunity to study the microstructure, dynamics, and stresses in gels that can lead to microcracks, an important problem that, for example, could affect 3D printer inks.
_source.Approach: The ACE-T4 experiment used confocal microscopy to observe the gels over a range of particle packing-fractions (temperatures), using pure, monodisperse poly(N -isopropylacrylamide) (pNIPA) particles in one sample, and then mixtures of pNIPAM particles with different amounts of particle dopants in five other samples. All of the samples formed gels. There was no crystallization in any sample . The data obtained permits the study of 3D gels with and without dopants as a function of temperature; the temperature changes vary the particle size and thus properties of the gels. In addition to the revised ACE-T4 experiment, ground-based soft matter research was completed and published.
_source.Hypothesis: The ACE-T4 experiments were intended to explore the transformation between a crystal and a glass by varying the density and character of particle dopants in three dimensional colloidal crystals. The original hypothesis stated that ''dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered (polycrystalline) solids and glasses with novel mechanical properties. Direct visualization of the evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity will provide fundamental insight into the nature of glasses and into processes such as nucleation and melting.''
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: By frustrating their structural order, the transition from ordered (crystal) to disordered (glassy) materials can alter the macroscopic behavior of ordered materials. Moreover, these experiments could also provide fundamental insight into the nature of nucleation, aging, and melting in materials with varying degrees of order. This information could benefit observation and synthesis of new colloidal materials (e.g. g., meta and photonic materials) for many applications ranging from color control to random laser.

_source.Title: Constrained Vapor Bubble
_source.Keywords: Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) Experiment     Heat Pipe Technology     Capillary Action     Phase change     Microgravity     Marangoni Flow     Internal Radiation
_source.Objectives:
The immediate macroscopic objectives are to determine the overall stability, the fluid flow characteristics, the average heat transfer coefficient in the evaporator, and the heat conductance of the CVB as a function of vapor volume and heat flow rate.
On the microscopic scale, the scientific objective is to evaluate the local details of the Kelvin-Clapeyron model of change-of-phase heat transfer under microgravity conditions where the extended Young-Laplace equation predominates.
_source.Approach:
The CVB-1 investigation used a variety of methods to study the behavior of the constrained vapor bubble (CVB) in a microgravity environment. This approach involved conducting experiments, creating mathematical models, and using insights from past CVB experiments to analyze the findings after the flight.

1. Experimental Design and Testing:
    -Customized CVB Cells: Five CVB cells were fabricated from quartz. Each cell featured a square cross-section (3 x 3 mm) and varying lengths to achieve specific liquid-to-vapor volume ratios. One cell was a ''dry'' cell, evacuated to
    5 torr, to establish baseline thermal behavior. The remaining four cells were filled with either pentane (a completely wetting fluid) or ethanol (a partially wetting fluid) before launch. Three cells utilized pentane at different volume
    ratios, while one was intended for ethanol.
    -Controlled Thermal Environment: The CVB cells were integrated into a system that allowed for precise control of heat input at the evaporator end and heat rejection at the condenser end. The system maintained a stable and
    uniform thermal environment for the cells.
    -Microgravity Environment: The CVB experiments were conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) to provide the necessary microgravity conditions.

2. Data Acquisition:
    -Macroscopic Measurements: Throughout the experiment, macroscopic data were recorded, including temperature profiles along the cell, vapor pressure, heat input and rejection rates, and visual observations of the vapor bubble.
    These observations were used to assess the overall performance and stability of the CVB system.
    -Microscopic Measurements: The investigation utilized an Image Analyzing Interferometer (IAI) to acquire detailed, microscopic measurements of the liquid film profile. These measurements included curvature profiles, film thickness
    profiles, and adsorbed film thickness. These data were crucial for understanding the local transport processes within the CVB.
    -Acceleration Measurements: The system monitored residual accelerations to assess their potential impact on the CVB's stability and behavior.
    Time Correlation: All acquired data were meticulously time-correlated to ensure accurate analysis and interpretation.

3. Mathematical Modeling and Analysis:
   - Extended Young-Laplace Equation: This equation, incorporating both capillary and van der Waals forces, was employed to model the equilibrium shape of the liquid-vapor interface.
    Kelvin-Clapeyron Transport Model: This model was used to analyze the non-equilibrium behavior of the CVB. It incorporated conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy, along with the extended Young-Laplace
    equation. The model was considered for refinement to account for internal radiative heat transfer, observed in previous experiments.
    -Numerical Modeling: Two- and three-dimensional numerical thermal modeling were considered to evaluate and refine the Kelvin-Clapeyron model, particularly to capture the complex interplay between capillary and Marangoni
    convection.
    -Internal Heat Analysis: Temperature data were analyzed to quantify the contributions of conduction, external radiation, and internal radiation to the overall heat transfer within the CVB system. This analysis built upon previous
    ground-based studies and included a detailed examination of the role of Marangoni convection.

4. Comparison with Ground-Based Studies:
    -Equilibrium Studies: The microgravity equilibrium data, including film thickness and curvature profiles, were compared with ground-based measurements to confirm the validity of the extended Young-Laplace equation under these
    conditions.
    -Non-Equilibrium Studies: Comparison of microgravity non-equilibrium data with results from ground-based studies illuminated the influence of gravity on CVB behavior. Specifically, this comparison focused on the differences in flow
    field symmetry and the magnitude of heat transfer.

5. Stability Analysis:
    -Macroscopic Stability: The investigation evaluated the overall stability of the CVB system, considering the occurrence of dryout, oscillations, and cavitation, as a function of heat flux, liquid-to-vapor volume ratio, and working fluid.
    -Microscopic Stability: A stability analysis was performed, leveraging experimental observations and mathematical modeling, to understand the conditions and mechanisms that lead to instability within the thin liquid film.

6. Post-Flight Analysis:
    -Reflectivity and Image Data: Detailed analysis of the raw reflectivity and image data was conducted to extract information about the adsorbed film thickness and its influence on CVB behavior.
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that the isothermal equilibrium liquid film shape depends on the gravitational field and the intermolecular force field which changes rapidly in the vicinity of the liquid-vapor and liquid-solid interfaces. This equilibrium shape in a particular gravitational field can be controlled by fixing the container shape, the liquid-substrate system, and the relative volume of the liquid to that of the vapor. It is further hypothesized that the extended Young-Laplace equation can describe this shape over a large range of conditions. Under non-equilibrium conditions resulting from an imposed temperature gradient, fluid flow and change-of-phase heat transfer are a function of further changes in the shape of the liquid volume. It is postulated that these non-equilibrium effects can be analyzed using a Kelvin-Clapeyron transport model that includes the use of the conservation of heat, mass and momentum and the extended Young-Laplace equation.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: CVB has performed ground-based studies in a thermal vacuum chamber to determine the efficiency of the heater and cooler configuration. Large thermal response times that have been experimentally observed in space-based experiments cannot be obtained from these ground-based studies. Space-based experimentation is the only method available to ascertain internal low-gravity fluid mechanics within a heat pipe. The project aims to achieve an improved understanding of microscale heat transfer, improved designs for wickless heat pipes, and an increased efficiency in heat transfer devices for cooling critical components. Targeted users are existing microelectronics industry and perhaps military applications. New designs should be able to be developed several months following the analysis and presentation of the results from the experiment.

_source.Objectives:
The proposed research aims to develop an integrated two-phase flow boiling/condensation facility for the International Space Station (ISS) to serve as a primary platform for obtaining two-phase flow and heat transfer data in microgravity. By comparing the microgravity data against those obtained in Earth’s gravity, it will be possible to ascertain the influence of body force on two-phase transport phenomena in pursuit of mechanistic models as well as correlations, and to help determine the minimum flow criteria to ensure gravity independent flow boiling and condensation. This research is a joint effort between the Purdue University Boiling and Two-Phase Flow Laboratory (PU-BTPFL) and the NASA Glenn Research Center. Personnel from the two organizations combine extensive experience in research and development of both flow boiling and condensation systems, and in conducting microgravity experiments.

The objectives of the Flow Boiling and the Flow Condensation Experiment (FBCE) in the long duration microgravity environment of the ISS are to:
    1. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity flow boiling critical heat flux (CHF) and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent CHF.
    2. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity annular condensation and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent annular condensation. Also, develop correlations for other condensation regimes in microgravity.
    3. Obtain flow boiling data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well characterized heating surface as functions of liquid inlet mass velocity and subcooling.
    4. Obtain flow condensation data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well-characterized condensing surface as functions of inlet quality and flow rate of condensing vapor. Specific tasks for the study will be as follows.
_source.Approach:
The approach used in this project is to perform the following sequential series of tasks:
1. Provide detailed design and instrumentation requirements for the Flow Boiling Module (FBM).
2. Provide design and instrumentation requirements for the entire flow loop.
3. Generate test matrix for operating conditions of the study.
4. Perform initial validation tests in both terrestrial gravity and parabolic flight.
5. Perform tests on board the ISS.
6. Based on both the ISS and terrestrial data, develop a series of predictive tools, including empirical correlations as well as theoretical, computational, and machine learning models.
_source.Hypothesis: In literature spanning many decades, body force in terrestrial gravity is identified as having a profound influence on two-phase transport behavior. This behavior is drastically altered In the absence of gravity, wherein flow fluid and heat transfer are dictated by flow inertia and surface tension. This implies predictive tools from terrestrial gravity studies are inapplicable for design of NASA's reduced gravity systems. This limitation points to a need for performing two-phase flow and heat transfer experiments on board the ISS as basis for formulating relevant reduced gravity predictive tools.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The proposed research will lay the foundation for development of advanced high power to weight ratio thermal management systems for NASA's future space vehicles and planetary bases.  Purdue University research has also shown tremendous value in findings from this projects to numerous other applications including ultra-fast charging of electric vehicles, fusion reactors, hydrogen storage, avionics, high-Mach turbine engines, and advanced electronics in laser, microwave, and radar systems.
